title: 413. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Unit Circle Coordinates at Standard Angles
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: State how the coordinates of a unit-circle point relate to cosine and sine.
questions.question: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position meets the unit circle at a point \(P\). What are the coordinates of \(P\)?
questions.explanation: On the unit circle the \(x\)-coordinate of the point is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\). For example, \(\theta=0\) gives the point \((1,0)\), which matches \((\cos 0,\sin 0)\) and not \((\sin 0,\cos 0)=(0,1)\).
questions.hint: Test both orders with \(\theta=0\), where the point is on the positive \(x\)-axis.

questions.concept: Unit-circle point at a quarter turn
questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle point for a quadrantal angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)?
questions.explanation: A rotation of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) from the positive \(x\)-axis reaches the positive \(y\)-axis, so the point is \((0,1)\). Indeed \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1\). The point \((1,0)\) corresponds to the angle \(0\).
questions.hint: Picture a quarter turn counterclockwise starting from \((1,0)\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle coordinates for a standard first-quadrant angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\)?
questions.explanation: The coordinates are \(\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6},\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)\). The angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) is small, so the point is close to the \(x\)-axis and its \(x\)-coordinate is the larger one. The other point corresponds to \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).
questions.hint: A small angle gives a point near the \(x\)-axis, so its \(y\)-coordinate is the smaller value.

questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle coordinates for a standard second-quadrant angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\)?
questions.explanation: The angle \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) is in Quadrant II with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). In Quadrant II the \(x\)-coordinate is negative and the \(y\)-coordinate is positive, so the point is \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\). The other point lies in Quadrant IV and corresponds to \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\).
questions.hint: Find the quadrant first to fix the signs, then use the reference angle for the sizes.

questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle coordinates for a standard third-quadrant angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\)?
questions.explanation: The angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) is in Quadrant III with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Both coordinates are negative, with sizes \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). The point is \(\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\). The other point corresponds to \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\), whose reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: Subtract \(\pi\) to find the reference angle, then attach the signs for Quadrant III.

questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle coordinates for a standard fourth-quadrant angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\)?
questions.explanation: The angle \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) is in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(2\pi-\frac{11\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{6}\). In Quadrant IV the \(x\)-coordinate is positive and the \(y\)-coordinate is negative, giving \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)\). The point with the opposite signs lies in Quadrant II and corresponds to \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: The angle is just short of a full turn, so the point lies just below the positive \(x\)-axis.

questions.concept: Unit-circle point at a half turn
questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle point for the angle pi.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(\pi\)?
questions.explanation: A half turn from the positive \(x\)-axis reaches the negative \(x\)-axis, so the point is \((-1,0)\); that is, \(\cos\pi=-1\) and \(\sin\pi=0\). The point \((0,-1)\) is reached after three quarters of a turn, at the angle \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
questions.hint: A half turn reverses the direction of the starting ray along the \(x\)-axis.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the angle in one full turn that corresponds to a given unit-circle point.
questions.question: Which angle \(\theta\) with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) corresponds to the unit-circle point \(\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\)?
questions.explanation: The \(x\)-coordinate is positive and the \(y\)-coordinate is negative, so the point is in Quadrant IV. The sizes \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) belong to the reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\), so \(\theta=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{5\pi}{3}\). The angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) is in Quadrant III, where the \(x\)-coordinate is negative.
questions.hint: Use the signs of the coordinates to find the quadrant, then match the sizes to a reference angle.

questions.concept: Unit-circle point for a negative angle
questions.learningObjective: Find the unit-circle coordinates for a negative standard angle.
questions.question: Which point of the unit circle corresponds to the angle \(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\)?
questions.explanation: A negative angle is measured clockwise. Rotating clockwise by \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) ends in Quadrant III, the same position as \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\), where both coordinates are negative. The point is \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\). The other point corresponds to the positive angle \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\).
questions.hint: Rotate clockwise from \((1,0)\), or add \(2\pi\) to obtain a coterminal positive angle.

questions.concept: Angles with a given vertical coordinate
questions.learningObjective: Find all angles in one full turn whose unit-circle point has a given second coordinate.
questions.question: For which angles \(\theta\) with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) does the corresponding unit-circle point have \(y\)-coordinate \(-\frac{1}{2}\)?
questions.explanation: The \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\), which is negative in Quadrants III and IV. The size \(\frac{1}{2}\) belongs to the reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(\theta=\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{7\pi}{6}\) or \(\theta=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{11\pi}{6}\). At \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) the \(y\)-coordinate is \(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
questions.hint: Decide which quadrants have a negative \(y\)-coordinate, then find the reference angle whose sine is \(\frac{1}{2}\).
